system:
You audit the knowledge atoms of one Knowledge Card. A card is the answer key for a benchmark of expert conceptual knowledge, so every atom must be correct, self-contained, and assessable on its own.

Judge every atom on every check listed below. Rules:
- For checks about evidence, use only the evidence sentences supplied with the atom. Do not repair an atom with your own knowledge.
- For GROUNDED, use "hold" when unreadable PDF symbols prevent verification; explain what is needed. Use fail only when the available evidence is sufficient to determine that the claim is unsupported. This hold rule takes precedence over the strictness rule. Judge other checks independently using their listed values; do not invent missing facts.
- Be strict within each check's allowed values. Do not turn an inability to verify GROUNDED into revise or fail; use hold as defined above.
- "why" is required for every value other than the first listed value; keep it under 30 words. Omit "why" when passing.

Checks (allowed values in brackets; the first value means no problem):
- GROUNDED [pass / revise / fail / hold]: The cited evidence sentences state the atom, including its specificity, causal force, assumptions, and certainty. pass = fully stated. revise = partly stated (the atom adds, drops, or strengthens something; say what). fail = not stated when the available evidence permits a judgment. hold = unreadable symbols prevent verification. For pass or revise, put the supporting evidence ids in cite.
- SINGLE_CLAIM [pass / revise]: The atom is one independently assessable claim. revise = it joins two or more claims that could be true or false separately. Evidence spanning more than three sentences is not by itself a reason to split or revise an atom.
- SCOPE_LABEL [pass / revise]: The S label fits (S1 what it is / S2 how it works / S3 where it ends). revise = wrong label; put the right one in why, e.g. 'S2: ...'.
- L1_ONLY [pass / fail]: The atom is recall-level knowledge. fail = knowing it requires applying the concept to a new problem, or combining facts from distant passages.
- SOURCE_INDEPENDENT [pass / revise / fail]: A domain expert who never read this book could judge the claim true or false. revise = phrased as the authors' statement but the claim itself is general (drop the attribution). fail = an isolated study finding, conjecture, or author-specific opinion, classification, or recommendation, even if attribution was removed. Explicitly scoped established facts about a formalism or architecture and conditional theoretical results remain eligible.
- NO_OVERLAP [pass / fail]: No other atom in this card states or contains the same claim. If two atoms overlap, fail only the less informative one and put the other atom's id in cite; the other one passes.
- CENTRALITY [pass / fail]: The atom matters for understanding the concept. fail = peripheral detail.
Whole-card checks (report under "batch"):
- CONCEPT_SCOPE [pass / fail]: The concept is a general concept of the field. fail = a topic whose assessable content is restricted to excluded study-specific findings or author-specific positions. A named formalism, system, or architecture is not disqualified solely for being specific if its scoped conceptual facts are source-independent.

Output ONLY one JSON object:
{"units": {"<atom_id>": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": "", "cite": []}, ...}, ...}, "batch": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": ""}}}

CONCEPT: Heterogeneous speed scaling
ASSESSMENT SCOPE: Deadline-based speed scaling on power-heterogeneous processors. Covers the optimal-schedule properties (hypopower), the flow-based offline algorithm, and the AVR-based online competitiveness.

ATOMS:
- CS-ALG-C05-S1-01 | S1
  ATOM: In deadline-based heterogeneous speed scaling, m power-heterogeneous processors $P_1,\dots,P_m$ are given, each processor $P_p$ has its own power function $f_p(s)$ depending on its speed $s$, and job preemption and migration are allowed.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0209-s23] In [7 SPP,8 SPP] we focus again on classical deadline-based scheduling and assume that m power-heterogeneous processors P1,...,Pm are given.
    [CS-ALG-p0209-s24] Let fp(s), 1 ≤p ≤m, be the power function of processor Pp, depending on speed s.
    [CS-ALG-p0209-s30] We assume that job preemption and migration is allowed.
- CS-ALG-C05-S1-02 | S1
  ATOM: Under general power functions, each processor's power function $f_p(s)$ is an arbitrary continuous and monotonically increasing function of the speed $s$.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0209-s26] 1.
    [CS-ALG-p0209-s27] General power functions: The function fp(s) of each processor Pp is an arbitrary continuous and monotonically increasing function of s. 2.
- CS-ALG-C05-S1-03 | S1
  ATOM: Under standard power functions, each processor P_p has power function $f_p(s)=s^{\alpha_p}$ with constant $\alpha_p>1$, and $\alpha=\max_{1\le p\le m}\alpha_p$.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0209-s28] Standard power functions: Each processor Pp has a power function of the form fp(s) = sαp, where αp > 1 is a constant.
    [CS-ALG-p0209-s29] Let α = max1≤p≤m αp.
- CS-ALG-C05-S2-01 | S2
  ATOM: For standard power functions, some optimal schedule executes each job $J_j$ with a constant hypopower $Q_j=f_p'(s_{j,p})$. If $J_j$ runs on processors $P_p$ and $P_q$ at speeds $s_{j,p}$ and $s_{j,q}$, then $f_p'(s_{j,p})=f_q'(s_{j,q})$, which follows from the convexity of the power functions.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0211-s08] More speciﬁ- cally, if Jj is partially executed by processors Pp and Pq with speeds s j,p and s j,q, respec- tively, then f p(s′ j,p) = f q(s′ j,q).
    [CS-ALG-p0211-s10] Therefore, for any job Jj, let Qj = f p(s′ j,p) be the hypopower on processor Pp.
    [CS-ALG-p0211-s11] Property 1: Each job Jj is executed with constant hypopower Qj.
- CS-ALG-C05-S2-02 | S2
  ATOM: The offline heterogeneous problem with standard power functions can be solved in polynomial time by a fully combinatorial algorithm based on repeated maximum flow computations.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0211-s04] As a main result in [7 SPP,8 SPP] we prove that the ofﬂine problem can be solved in polynomial time using a fully com- binatorial algorithm that is based on repeated maximum ﬂow computations.
- CS-ALG-C05-S2-03 | S2
  ATOM: A schedule on heterogeneous processors is called an AVR-schedule if, for every job J_j and every unit interval I_t \subseteq [r_j,d_j), the total work of J_j executed during I_t on all processors equals the job's density \delta_j.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0213-s21] Based on the above algorithm variation, we say that a schedule S is an AVR-schedule if, for every job Jj and interval It ⊆[r j,dj), the total amount of work of Jj executed during It on all the processors in S is equal to δj.
- CS-ALG-C05-S2-04 | S2
  ATOM: In the offline algorithm for standard power functions, feasibility of running all jobs at one common hypopower $Q$ is decided by a maximum flow computation. If no feasible schedule with hypopower $Q$ exists, the instance is partitioned into two independent subproblems, $(J_{\ge Q},P_{\ge Q},I)$ and $(J_{<Q},P_{<Q},I)$.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0212-s04] As we will explain below, this feasibility problem and the calculation of the corresponding schedule can be solved using a maximum ﬂow computation.
    [CS-ALG-p0212-s05] If such a feasible schedule does not exist, then (J,P,I) can be partitioned into two independent subproblems (J≥Q,P≥Q,I) and (J<Q,P<Q,I).
- CS-ALG-C05-S3-01 | S3
  ATOM: The offline algorithm for standard power functions assumes that every job density satisfies $\delta_j \ge \max_{p,q}(\alpha_p/\alpha_q)^{1/(\alpha_q-1)}$; under this assumption an optimal schedule has all speeds $s_{j,p}\ge 1$, which allows the processors to be ordered from cheaper to more expensive.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0211-s14] We assume that the density δj := wj/(dj −r j) of each job Jj satisﬁes δj ≥maxp,q(αp/αq)1/(αq−1).
    [CS-ALG-p0211-s16] With the assumption on the job densities we can then show that in an optimal schedule, for each job Jj and processor Pp, the speed s j,p is at least 1.
    [CS-ALG-p0211-s17] This allows us to deﬁne an order on the processors.
- CS-ALG-C05-S3-02 | S3
  ATOM: The linear-programming approach for general power functions applies to continuous power functions satisfying the invariant that, for any small \epsilon>0, there is an \epsilon'>0 with f((1+\epsilon)s)\le(1+\epsilon')f(s) for all s\in[s_{LB},s_{UB}], and it yields only a (1+\epsilon')-approximate schedule rather than an exact optimum.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0210-s11] We consider the wide class of continuous power functions satisfying the following invariant.
    [CS-ALG-p0210-s12] For any small constant ε > 0, there exists a small value ε′ > 0 such that f((1+ε)s) ≤(1+ε′)f(s) holds for any speed s ∈[sLB,sUB].
    [CS-ALG-p0210-s22] There exists an algorithm that produces a (1 + ε′)-approximate schedule in O(poly(n,m, ε1 ,log( sUBSLB )) time.
